title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize K–12 mathematics instruction. The central question is how teachers interact with ChatGPT when adapting existing curriculum tasks to students’ interests, and whether that process is efficient, pedagogically sound, and appealing to students.

The study involved 7 middle school mathematics teachers in the United States who used GPT-4o / ChatGPT to modify problems from the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum. Teachers personalized problems for popular-culture interest areas, iteratively prompting the model during recorded Zoom sessions and then assigning the resulting problems to 521 seventh-grade students via ASSISTments. Teachers received a 2-hour training session before implementation, and the same procedure was repeated in two different units so the researchers could examine changes over time.

Results show that teachers commonly used prompts to adjust the specificity of interests, realism, numerical appropriateness, readability, and age-appropriateness. Students generally preferred finer-grained, more specific references, while teachers often worked to repair shallow or unrealistic AI output. Personalizing one problem took about 4 minutes on average, and this did not become clearly more efficient across iterations; in fact, teachers used more prompts and more time in the second unit, though student ratings also improved. The paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can improve instructional quality and provide professional learning, but it is still time-consuming and may not align well with students’ desire for more individualized, fine-grained personalization.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative AI chatbot/LLM system used to generate and revise text-based outputs through prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Seven middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT (with underlying model GPT-4o) to personalize existing Illustrative Mathematics problems for students’ interests and to iteratively revise the problems over two units.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers spent an average of 246 seconds (about 4 minutes) to pose each of 143 personalized problems, using 558 prompts in total (average 3.2 prompts per problem). Efficiency did not clearly improve over time: from Unit 4 to Unit 6, teachers used significantly more prompts and more time per problem, although student ratings of interestingness and closeness also increased.
findings.measure: Teacher time per problem; number of prompts per problem; student ratings of interestingness and closeness
findings.effect_size: B=1.26 (prompts per problem from Unit 4 to Unit 6); B=70.4 seconds (time per problem from Unit 4 to Unit 6); B=0.33 for student ratings increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6; B=0.240 for 3-5 prompts vs other prompt counts
findings.sample_size: teachers n=7; students n=521; problems n=143

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study with direct teacher use in authentic classrooms, but it is not an experimental comparison and has no control group for learning outcomes. Evidence is informative but largely observational and exploratory.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports small-to-modest differences in student ratings and mixed efficiency findings, but it does not demonstrate a clear positive or negative instructional impact on achievement. The most salient result is that teacher-in-the-loop personalization remained time-consuming and did not become more efficient over time.
